summary: Describes the Internet Control Message Protocol, which lets gateways and hosts report errors and exchange simple diagnostic information about how datagrams are handled. This early edition was replaced by the final specification. Replaced by RFC 792.

plainLanguage.summary: When a letter cannot be delivered, the post office sends a note saying why. ICMP is how internet machines send such notes to each other.

subtitle: Early specification for reporting IP errors and control information

tldr.problem: IP datagrams can fail to reach their destination, routers need to reject datagrams, and hosts need to request better routes, but IP itself provides no way to report these conditions.
tldr.mechanism: ICMP sends control messages from gateways and hosts back to the source IP address when problems occur, using type codes for different conditions: unreachable, time exceeded, parameter problem, source quench, redirect, echo, and timestamp.
tldr.outcome: This was an early version of ICMP that was replaced by RFC 792, the final specification still in use.

facts.label: Encapsulation
facts.value: Uses IP header with returned datagram header plus 64 bits of data

today: RFC 777 is a historic early version of ICMP that was superseded by RFC 792, which became the standard Internet Control Message Protocol specification.

sections.title: Purpose and Design
sections.content:
RFC 777 specifies the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), which is used by gateways and hosts to report errors and exchange diagnostic information about how IP datagrams are processed. ICMP is not designed to make IP reliable; rather, it provides feedback about problems so that higher-level protocols can implement their own reliability if needed.

ICMP messages are sent when a datagram cannot reach its destination, when a gateway lacks buffering capacity, when a route can be optimized, or when fragments cannot be reassembled in time. Importantly, no ICMP messages are sent about ICMP messages themselves, to avoid infinite regress.
sections.plainLanguage: ICMP lets routers and computers tell the sender when something goes wrong with a message. It is just a way to report problems, not to fix them.

sections.title: Message Types and Formats
sections.content:
ICMP messages use the IP header with specific protocol number (ICMP = 1) and include a type field that determines the rest of the message format. RFC 777 defines eight message types:

Destination Unreachable (Type 3) reports that a network, host, protocol, or port is unreachable, or that fragmentation is needed but the Don't Fragment flag is set. Time Exceeded (Type 11) signals either that the time-to-live counter reached zero or that fragment reassembly timed out. Parameter Problem (Type 12) indicates an invalid option or header parameter. Source Quench (Type 4) tells the sender to reduce traffic rate when a gateway approaches capacity.

Redirect (Type 5) advises a host to use a better gateway for a particular network. Echo (Type 8) and Echo Reply (Type 0) enable simple ping-like diagnostics by echoing data back. Timestamp (Type 13) and Timestamp Reply (Type 14) carry millisecond timestamps for network timing measurements.
sections.plainLanguage: ICMP has eight different message types: some report problems, some ask for replies to test connectivity, some carry timing information, and some suggest better routes.

sections.title: When Messages Are Sent
sections.content:
ICMP Destination Unreachable is sent when a gateway's routing tables show a network is unreachable, when a destination host lacks an active protocol module for the requested service, or when a datagram must be fragmented but carries the Don't Fragment flag. Time Exceeded is sent when a gateway discards a datagram because its time-to-live field is zero, or when a host cannot reassemble fragments within its time limit.

Parameter Problem is sent when a gateway or host encounters an unimplemented option or corrupt header. Source Quench can be sent proactively when a gateway approaches capacity, allowing the sender to rate-limit traffic before packets are actually dropped. Redirect is sent when a host sends traffic through a suboptimal gateway that could be reached directly. Echo and Timestamp messages are used voluntarily for diagnostics and network synchronization.
sections.plainLanguage: Different situations trigger different messages: when something cannot be reached, when time runs out, when the header is bad, when the router is too busy, when a better route exists, or when testing connectivity.

items.label: Destination Unreachable
items.desc: Network, host, protocol, or port unreachable; or fragmentation needed with DF set.

items.label: Source Quench
items.desc: Gateway congestion; sender should reduce transmission rate.

items.label: Redirect
items.desc: Gateway suggests a better route for the destination.

items.label: Echo
items.desc: Request for echo reply to test connectivity.

items.label: Time Exceeded
items.desc: TTL reached zero or fragment reassembly timeout.

items.label: Parameter Problem
items.desc: Invalid or unimplemented option in header.
